notes:
Scope: researchers, identity-system designers and privacy thinkers whose largely online work shaped the privacy debate on the line that leads to person-held terms — re-identification (Sweeney; Narayanan & Shmatikov), machine-readable notice and the cost of consent (Cranor; McDonald), browser-sent preferences (Soghoian's Do Not Track), design-side and contextual theories (Cavoukian; Nissenbaum; boyd; Zuboff), and the user-centric identity / VRM line (Cameron; Kaliya Young; Searls; Christopher Allen; Berners-Lee's Solid). 15 people, 13 events, 6 myths, 12 openly licensed portraits. Method: one person at a time; every quote was copied from text printed by tools/fetch-text.py and re-checked with --check at the end (114 source objects, all CONFIRMED). Five quotes from Christopher Soghoian's Blogger site and dubfire.net return NOT-FOUND from fetch-text.py only because its paragraph extractor skips div/
text; they were verified against the same fetched HTML's full get_text() and each source note says so. Some PDFs' text layers use 'fi'/'ff' ligatures, which are kept in the quotes so they match. Portrait licences were read from the Commons API extmetadata (and file wikitext where the metadata conflicted); thumbnails are saved as JPEG q82 in assets/media. Corrections to the brief: (1) the first Internet Identity Workshop (26–27 Oct 2005) met in Berkeley (Hillside Club), not Mountain View — IIW moved to the Computer History Museum later (see myth); (2) McDonald & Cranor's published paper gives a point estimate of 244 hours a year to read policies (Table 7) while its conclusion says 'approximately 201 hours' — both are recorded; (3) the Privacy by Design resolution (Jerusalem, 27–29 Oct 2010) is NOT written as an event here because global.json already has it as jerusalem-resolution-privacy-by-design-2010; it is cited in Cavoukian's card. Overlaps for the editorial layer to resolve: latanya-sweeney also appears in personas-code.json and doc-searls in personas-advocates.json; myterms.json has projectvrm-launched-berkman-2006 (duplicate of searls-projectvrm-launched-berkman-2006) and P3P / Do Not Track as lineage items (this file has them as events w3c-p3p-recommendation-2002 and soghoian-stamm-do-not-track-header-prototype-2009). Could not read by script: doc.searls.com, projectvrm.org and blogs.harvard.edu/vrm (403), identitywoman.net (captcha), medium.com, several w3.org pages (403 intermittently), web.archive.org (connection resets for most of the session), IPC Ontario's own Privacy by Design PDF (a Simon Fraser University copy was used), The Baffler and OneZero (critiques of Zuboff by Morozov and Doctorow — mentioned only in a note, not cited). Known gaps: no openly licensed portraits found on Commons for Vitaly Shmatikov, Aleecia McDonald or Christopher Allen; Kim Cameron's portrait is a group photo (with Drummond Reed and Esther Dyson); Kaliya Young's is a wide workshop shot. Cynthia Dwork (differential privacy) and Ashkan Soltani are covered in other persona slices and were not duplicated. The first use of 'VRM' (reportedly a Gillmor Gang podcast, 1 Sept 2006) and the ProjectVRM launch month were not verified — the event is dated 2006 only.

keyWork.title: Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely (Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3)

people.contribution: As an MIT graduate student in 1997, Sweeney linked a $20 Cambridge voter list to Massachusetts state-employee health data released without names, and picked out Governor William Weld's hospital record. Her 2000 working paper estimated from 1990 Census data that 87% of the U.S. population was likely unique on five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth, and her 2002 k-anonymity model proposed a formal test for releases. She later founded Harvard's Data Privacy Lab and served as the Federal Trade Commission's chief technologist.

people.name: Lorrie Faith Cranor
people.roles: computer scientist · usable-privacy researcher · P3P co-author · FTC chief technologist (2016)

keyWork.title: The Platform for Privacy Preferences 1.0 (P3P1.0) Specification, W3C Recommendation (co-author, then at AT&T)

people.contribution: Cranor was one of the authors of P3P, the W3C standard (Recommendation, 16 April 2002) that let websites publish their privacy practices in a machine-readable format for browsers to read on users' behalf. At Carnegie Mellon she directs the CyLab Usable Privacy and Security Laboratory and founded the Symposium On Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS); with Aleecia McDonald she estimated in 2008 that reading the privacy policy of every new site an American visits would take about 244 hours a year. In 2012 she published a candid post-mortem of P3P and of notice-and-choice, and in 2016 she served as chief technologist at the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.
people.quote: P3P is a user empowerment tool that was developed in response to Congressional and FTC interest in online privacy in the mid-1990s and concerns that it was unrealistic to expect consumers to read long online privacy policies at every website they visit.

He thanked participants including Doc Searls, Kaliya ('Identity Woman'), Caspar Bowden and Stefan Brands, and used the laws to explain the failures of Microsoft's own Passport system. He went on to work on Information Cards (CardSpace) and supported the Internet Identity Workshop from its first meeting in October 2005. He died in November 2021.

people.name: danah boyd
people.roles: ethnographer of networked life · founder of Data & Society

keyWork.title: It's Complicated: The Social Lives of Networked Teens (Yale University Press; open-access PDF)

people.contribution: boyd spent a decade studying how teenagers use social media and argued, against the claim that young people do not care about privacy, that they work hard to achieve it within public networks — often by controlling who can understand a post rather than who can see it. In talks such as 'Networked Privacy' (2011) she argued that privacy is collective: what friends, parents and data brokers share about us implicates us. She founded the Data & Society research institute and is now a professor of communication at Cornell.

people.name: Helen Nissenbaum
people.roles: philosopher of information · author of 'contextual integrity' · co-creator of TrackMeNot
people.place: New York City (New York University; Cornell Tech)

keyWork.title: Privacy as Contextual Integrity, 79 Washington Law Review 119

people.contribution: Nissenbaum proposed 'contextual integrity' (2004; expanded in her book Privacy in Context, Stanford University Press): privacy is violated when information flows break the norms of the context in which it was shared, rather than whenever something 'private' becomes known. With Daniel Howe at NYU she released TrackMeNot in August 2006, a browser extension that hides a user's real searches in a stream of decoy queries. She later co-wrote Obfuscation: A User's Guide for Privacy and Protest (2015, with Finn Brunton) and directs the Digital Life Initiative at Cornell Tech.
people.quote: Contextual integrity ties adequate protection for privacy to norms of specific contexts, demanding that information gathering and dissemination be appropriate to that context and obey the governing norms of distribution within it.

events.title: A graduate student finds the governor in 'anonymous' health data
events.place: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Massachusetts' Group Insurance Commission had released patient-level data on about 135,000 state employees and their families, believed to be anonymous, to researchers and sold a copy to industry. Latanya Sweeney, then an MIT graduate student, bought the Cambridge voter registration list for twenty dollars and linked it on ZIP code, birth date and gender. Governor William Weld's record stood out: six Cambridge voters shared his birth date, three were men, and only he lived in his five-digit ZIP code.
events.significance: It showed that stripping names is not the same as making data anonymous, a lesson that shaped HIPAA's de-identification rules and every later argument that people need a say over data 'about' them.

events.title: ZIP code, gender and birth date: the 87% estimate
events.summary: In a Carnegie Mellon working paper, Latanya Sweeney used 1990 U.S. Census summary data to estimate how many people had rare combinations of demographic values. She found that 87% of the population (216 million of 248 million) likely had a unique combination of five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth, and about half (53%) on place, gender and date of birth. A 2006 re-analysis of the 2000 Census by Philippe Golle put the ZIP–gender–birth-date figure at 63%.
events.significance: The number turned 'anonymised' into a claim that had to be proved, and it is still the most-quoted statistic in arguments that personal data needs the person's own controls.

events.title: Netflix's 'anonymous' ratings are matched to named people
events.place: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, Oakland, California
events.summary: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin presented a statistical attack on the Netflix Prize dataset, which held movie ratings of about 500,000 subscribers with names replaced by numbers. Using ratings people had posted publicly on the Internet Movie Database as background knowledge, they identified the Netflix records of known users. They calculated that eight ratings (two of which may be wrong) with dates accurate to 14 days single out 99% of records. In March 2010, after FTC staff raised the research with the company, Netflix suspended plans for a second prize dataset.
events.significance: It carried re-identification from demographics to behaviour — what people watch, click and buy — the very data online services collect, and it moved a regulator to act.

events.title: P3P: websites state their privacy practices in machine-readable form
events.place: World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), MIT Laboratory for Computer Science, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: After a process begun in 1997, the W3C published the Platform for Privacy Preferences (P3P 1.0) as a Recommendation on 16 April 2002; its authors included Lorrie Cranor of AT&T. Sites would publish machine-readable privacy policies and browsers would act on users' preferences without the user reading each policy. The originally planned negotiation protocol was dropped, the working group closed in 2006 for lack of industry participation, and W3C declared the specification obsolete on 30 August 2018.
events.significance: The first standard for machine-readable privacy terms — but the terms were the website's, read by the user's software, the mirror image of the person-proffered terms of IEEE 7012.

events.title: A browser header that says 'do not track'
events.place: Future of Privacy Forum meeting and conference call (FPF is based in Washington, D.C.)
events.summary: In July 2009 Christopher Soghoian and Sid Stamm built a prototype Firefox add-on that added 'X-Do-Not-Track: 1' and 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1' headers to every web request, replacing the per-company opt-out cookies that were erased whenever users cleared cookies. In mid-July Soghoian pitched the header at a Future of Privacy Forum meeting; none of the advertising firms showed interest. After FTC chairman Jon Leibowitz revived the 'do not track' idea in July 2010, the header approach displaced a 2007 advocacy proposal for an FTC-run Do Not Track list, and W3C later worked on it as the DNT standard until 2019.
events.significance: For the first time a person's own software stated a tracking preference to every site at once — the one-bit ancestor of machine-readable personal terms.

sources.institution: slight paranoia (Christopher Soghoian's blog)

sources.note: First-hand account. Verified against the fetched page's full text (the repo helper's extractor skips this Blogger post body). Same post: the 2007 groups 'asked the FTC to create a Do Not Track list for online advertising'; Leibowitz raised a 'do-not-track' list at a Senate Commerce Committee hearing on 27 July 2010; 'none of the advertising firms showed any interest in the header.'

events.title: Reading every privacy policy would take 244 hours a year
events.summary: Aleecia McDonald and Lorrie Faith Cranor of Carnegie Mellon measured how long privacy policies take to read and skim and multiplied by the number of sites Americans visit. Their point estimate was 244 hours a year per person to read the policy of each new site word-for-word — about 40 minutes a day — worth about $781 billion a year nationally in lost time. The paper's conclusion gives a lower figure of about 201 hours, which does not match its own tables.
events.significance: It put a number on why notice-and-consent fails: no one can read the terms, so the terms have to be read by machines — or set by the person.

sources.institution: I/S: A Journal of Law and Policy for the Information Society, vol. 4 no. 3 (2008 Privacy Year in Review); copy hosted by Stanford Center for Internet and Society
sources.title: A. M. McDonald and L. F. Cranor, 'The Cost of Reading Privacy Policies'
sources.quote: using the point estimate of 244 hours per year to read privacy policies per person means an average of 40 minutes a day.
sources.note: Same paper: 'the nation would lose the value of about $781 billion from the opportunity cost value of the time to read privacy policies.' Its conclusion says 'approximately 201 hours a year, worth about $3,534 annually per American Internet user'; Table 7 gives 244 hours (range 181-304) to read and 154 hours to skim.

sources.title: L. F. Cranor, 'Necessary But Not Sufficient: Standardized Mechanisms for Privacy Notice and Choice'
sources.quote: If an individual were to read the privacy policy at every website she visited even once per year, she would spend, on average, an estimated 244 hours per year reading privacy policies.

events.locationNote: Carnegie Mellon University (CyLab), where both authors worked.

events.title: Kim Cameron publishes 'The Laws of Identity'
events.summary: Kim Cameron, Microsoft's Architect of Identity, published seven 'Laws of Identity' after refining them in public on his Identityblog. The first law, 'User Control and Consent', holds that identity systems must reveal identifying information only with the user's consent; the second calls for minimal disclosure for a constrained use. Cameron argued the laws explained the failures of Microsoft's own Passport identity system.
events.significance: A major platform company's identity architect put user control and consent at the base of Internet identity design — the premise from which user-held credentials and person-proffered terms grew.

sources.institution: Kim Cameron, Microsoft Corporation (Identityblog)
sources.title: The Laws of Identity
sources.quote: Technical identity systems must only reveal information identifying a user with the user’s consent.
sources.note: The PDF is headed '…as of 5/11/2005'; the URL path is dated 13 May 2005. Law 2 is 'Minimal Disclosure for a Constrained Use'. The text says the Law of Justifiable Parties can 'account for the successes and failures of Microsoft‟s Passport identity system'.

sources.institution: Phil Windley, Technometria

sources.quote: Kim Cameron's Laws of Identity are a foundational work in online identity.

events.locationNote: Microsoft's headquarters in Redmond, where Cameron worked; the laws were developed and published online (identityblog.com).

events.title: The first Internet Identity Workshop meets in Berkeley
events.summary: Kaliya Hamlin (now Young), Drummond Reed, Doc Searls and Phil Windley hosted the first Internet Identity Workshop in Berkeley on 26–27 October 2005 to compare proposals for Internet-wide identity, from Microsoft's InfoCard to OpenID and i-names. The first day opened with Searls on 'the rise of the fully empowered customer'; the second ran as a participant-driven 'structured open space' at the Hillside Club, at Hamlin's urging. One breakout discussed 'Identity Rights Agreements' — ways for users to state their privacy preferences — and concluded that what was missing was a legal framework to make such agreements binding.
events.significance: The user-centric identity community took shape here, and its 'Identity Rights Agreements' session posed, in 2005, the problem that person-proffered terms like IEEE 7012 set out to solve.

sources.institution: Phil Windley, Technometria (blog of an IIW co-founder)
sources.title: Announcing the Internet Identity Workshop (IIW2005)

sources.note: The announcement lists proposals to be compared, including 'Microsoft's InfoCard system', 'OpenID' and 'XRI/XDI (i-names)'.

sources.quote: What we're saying in the discussion of IRAs is that we can build systems that allow users to easily indicate their privacy preferences, at least for some classes of data. What's missing is the legal framework in the middle to make such agreements legally binding.

events.locationNote: The Hillside Club in Berkeley is named in Windley's day-two report (coordinates approximate). Later IIWs meet at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View.

events.title: ProjectVRM: tools for the customer's side of the relationship
events.place: Berkman Center for Internet & Society, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Doc Searls created ProjectVRM when he became a fellow at Harvard's Berkman Center in 2006. VRM — vendor relationship management — was framed as the customer-side counterpart of companies' CRM systems. Its principles hold that customers should control the data they generate, share it selectively, and 'proffer their own terms of engagement' with auditable records of agreements; Searls reported its progress in The Intention Economy (Harvard Business Review Press, 2012).
events.significance: This is where the idea of person-proffered terms was named and organised; IEEE 7012's own FAQ says the ideas behind the standard 'were worked out in ProjectVRM'.

events.title: The identity community turns to agents
events.place: Computer History Museum, Mountain View, California
events.summary: The day after the 41st Internet Identity Workshop, its organisers held the first Agentic Internet Workshop at the Computer History Museum. Run in the same open-space format, it had more than 40 sessions on agent identity protocols, agentic browsers, policy enforcement for AI agents and the legal frameworks for 'human-centric agency', with participants from 10 countries. Co-organiser Phil Windley framed it as a response to an internet where agents 'interact, negotiate, and make decisions on our behalf'.
events.significance: Twenty years after the first IIW asked how people could control their own identifiers, the same community began asking how people could control the agents that act for them — the setting in which person-proffered terms like MyTerms now operate.

sources.institution: Phil Windley, Technometria (IIW co-founder)
sources.title: The First Agentic Internet Workshop
sources.quote: On October 24, 2025, the day after IIW 41 wrapped up, we held the first-ever Agentic Internet Workshop (AIW1) at the Computer History Museum.
sources.note: Same post: 'IIW 41 was about the state of identity. AIW1 asked: what happens when we give identity the power to act?' and 'With more than 40 sessions across four time slots'.

sources.institution: Phil Windley, Technometria
sources.title: From IIW to the Agentic Internet Workshop
sources.quote: Together, we now face the shift toward an internet where agents—AI-powered and otherwise—interact, negotiate, and make decisions on our behalf.

events.locationNote: Computer History Museum, Mountain View (coordinates approximate), where IIW now meets.

events.title: TrackMeNot hides real searches in a cloud of decoys
events.place: New York University, New York City
events.summary: Daniel Howe and Helen Nissenbaum of New York University released TrackMeNot, a free Firefox extension that periodically sends randomised 'ghost' queries to search engines so that a user's real searches are harder to profile. Its authors cited the U.S. Justice Department's 2005 subpoena of search records and the New York Times coverage of AOL's release of search logs. By their count it passed 350,000 downloads; a 2010 study showed that a search engine using machine-learning classifiers could often separate the decoys from real queries.
events.significance: An early example of privacy as something users enact with their own software against a service, rather than a setting the service grants.

sources.institution: D. C. Howe and H. Nissenbaum, New York University — chapter in 'Lessons from the Identity Trail' (Oxford University Press); pre-publication PDF hosted by the TrackMeNot project
sources.title: TrackMeNot: Resisting Surveillance in Web Search
sources.quote: Since August 2006, when the initial version of TMN was made publicly available, free of charge, there have been over 350,000 downloads.
sources.note: The PDF is headed 'In: On the Identity Trail: Privacy, Anonymity and Identity in a Networked Society, Eds. Ian Kerr, Carole Lucock and Valerie Steeves (Forthcoming, Oxford University Press)'. sources.institution: TrackMeNot project, hosted at New York University
sources.title: TrackMeNot
sources.quote: It hides users' actual search trails in a cloud of 'ghost' queries, significantly increasing the difficulty of aggregating such data into accurate or identifying user profiles.
sources.note: The 'why we created TMN' section refers to the Justice Department subpoena to Google 'initiated August 2005' and to a front-page New York Times article on AOL's release of search data.

events.title: 'The Age of Surveillance Capitalism' names the business model
events.place: PublicAffairs (Hachette Book Group), New York City
events.summary: Harvard Business School professor emerita Shoshana Zuboff published The Age of Surveillance Capitalism in the United States on 15 January 2019, after a German edition in October 2018; she had written it from 2011 through 2018. The 704-page book describes an economic order in which once-private human experience is extracted as data and used to manufacture and sell predictions about behaviour. Its publisher billed it as an international bestseller, and its title term became a common name for the tracking-based business model.
events.significance: It recast tracking from a privacy nuisance into an economic system — sharpening the case that individuals need their own terms, not just better notices.

events.title: The web's inventor goes public with Solid personal data pods
events.place: MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Tim Berners-Lee published 'One Small Step for the Web…', announcing that he had been working with colleagues at MIT and elsewhere on Solid, 'an open-source project to restore the power and agency of individuals on the web', and that he was taking a sabbatical from MIT to found the company Inrupt with John Bruce. Solid, described in a 2016 MIT–Qatar Computing Research Institute paper, stores each person's data in a personal online datastore ('pod') they control, so they can switch apps and pod providers.
events.significance: The web's inventor proposed reversing its data architecture — people keep their data and grant access — the storage-side counterpart to people setting their own terms.

myths.claim: 87% of Americans can be identified from just their ZIP code, gender and date of birth.
myths.correction: Sweeney's 87% was an estimate from 1990 Census summary data of how many people 'likely' had a unique combination of five-digit ZIP, gender and birth date — not a count of people actually re-identified. Re-running the analysis on the 2000 Census, Philippe Golle found 63%. Actually naming someone also needs an outside list (such as a voter roll) that contains them; Barth-Jones argues that incomplete lists make many such matches uncertain. The core point — that a few ordinary attributes single out most people — survived the re-analysis.

sources.institution: Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3 (hosted by the Data Privacy Lab)
sources.title: L. Sweeney, Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely
sources.quote: It was found that 87% (216 million of 248 million) of the population in the United States had reported characteristics that likely made them unique based only on {5-digit ZIP, gender, date of birth}.
sources.note: The abstract says the experiments used '1990 U.S. Census summary data'.

sources.institution: Philippe Golle, Palo Alto Research Center — WPES '06 (author's copy, Stanford)
sources.title: Revisiting the Uniqueness of Simple Demographics in the US Population
sources.quote: Our results generally agree with the ﬁndings of [10], although we ﬁnd that disclosing one’s gender, ZIP code and full date of birth allows for unique identiﬁcation of fewer individuals (63% of the US population) than reported in [10].
sources.note: Text layer uses the 'fi' ligature.

sources.institution: Daniel C. Barth-Jones, Columbia University (SSRN 2076397; FPF copy)
sources.title: The 'Re-identification' of Governor William Weld's Medical Information: A Critical Re-examination
sources.quote: Weld was most likely re-identifiable only because he was a public figure who experienced a highly publicized hospitalization
sources.note: Barth-Jones's critique is itself disputed by re-identification researchers (e.g. Narayanan and Felten, 2014).

myths.claim: Christopher Soghoian invented Do Not Track, an anti-tracking tool that all major browsers use.
myths.correction: By Soghoian's own account the name came from a 2007 proposal by public-interest groups for an FTC-run 'Do Not Track list'; the idea of a browser header had been urged on him by Dan Kaminsky and Mozilla's Mike Shaver before he and Sid Stamm built the first header prototype in July 2009. DNT was a request, not a blocking tool: it only worked if sites chose to honour it, W3C closed the standard in January 2019 for lack of deployment, and in February 2019 Apple began removing it from Safari because the signal could itself be used to fingerprint users.

sources.title: The History of the Do Not Track Header
sources.quote: In 2007, several public interest groups, including the World Privacy Forum, CDT and EFF, asked the FTC to create a Do Not Track list for online advertising.
sources.note: Verified against the fetched page's full text. The same post quotes Kaminsky's email ('Just add an "X-No-Track: user-opt-out=explicit" header to all HTTP requests') and says Mozilla's VP of Engineering Mike Shaver 'emailed me to state his own preference for a header'.

myths.claim: The Internet Identity Workshop began in 2005 at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View.
myths.correction: IIW now meets at the Computer History Museum, and its site says it has met twice a year since 2005 — which invites the assumption. But the co-founders' own announcement and reports from the time place the first workshop, on 26–27 October 2005, in Berkeley, with the open-space day held at the Hillside Club.

myths.claim: OAuth was created at the Internet Identity Workshop.
myths.correction: Speaker biographies often say OAuth and OpenID Connect were 'created' at IIW. OAuth's own published history traces it to a November 2006 conversation between Twitter and Ma.gnolia developers at a CitizenSpace OpenID meeting, a Google group formed in April 2007 and a final OAuth Core 1.0 draft on 3 October 2007, without mentioning IIW. IIW was one of several forums where this user-centric identity work was discussed and advanced, as its co-founder Phil Windley says, rather than the place it was invented.

myths.claim: Young people who grew up online don't care about privacy.
myths.correction: Teens did share more about themselves as platforms grew — Pew found each of five kinds of personal information more widely posted in 2012 than in 2006 — but few took a fully public approach. Sixty per cent of teen Facebook users kept their profiles private and 74% of teen social-media users had deleted people from their networks. danah boyd's fieldwork found teens working to achieve privacy inside public networks, often by controlling who could understand a post rather than who could see it. What teens worried about least was third-party access: only 9% were 'very' concerned.

sources.institution: Pew Research Center (with the Berkman Center for Internet & Society)
sources.title: Teens, Social Media, and Privacy
sources.quote: However, few teens embrace a fully public approach to social media. Instead, they take an array of steps to restrict and prune their profiles
sources.note: Survey of 802 teens. Same page: '60% of teen Facebook users keep their profiles private'; '74% of teen social media users have deleted people from their network or friends list'; 'just 9% say they are “very” concerned' about third-party access to their data.

sources.quote: Teenagers have not given up on privacy, even if their attempts to achieve it are often undermined by people who hold power over them.

myths.claim: Shoshana Zuboff coined the term 'surveillance capitalism'.
myths.correction: Zuboff developed the best-known theory of surveillance capitalism and made the term famous with her 2019 book, and reviewers often credit her with coining it. But John Bellamy Foster and Robert W. McChesney had already published 'Surveillance Capitalism: Monopoly-Finance Capital, the Military-Industrial Complex, and the Digital Age' in the socialist magazine Monthly Review's July–August 2014 issue, with a different analysis centred on monopoly capital and the military-industrial complex. The phrase has more than one origin; Zuboff's meaning — the extraction of behavioural data to sell predictions — is her own.
